content: A peripheral venous catheter (PVC) is a medical device commonly used for short-term administration of fluids and medications directly into the bloodstream. It is one of the most frequently performed invasive procedures in hospitals. However, PVCs often fail before the completion of intravenous therapy. This failure can occur due to inadequate attachment of the catheter to the skin, which may result in the catheter falling out. Such dislodgement can lead to complications, including phlebitis (inflammation or irritation of the vein wall), infiltration (leakage of fluid into surrounding tissues), or occlusion (blockage of the catheter). Additionally, an improperly secured PVC increases the risk of catheter-related bloodstream infections (CRBSIs). This is because the pistoning motion of the catheter (movement back and forth within the vein) can facilitate the migration of microorganisms along the catheter and into the bloodstream. Despite the availability of various dressings and securement devices designed to stabilize PVCs, the effectiveness of different securement techniques in prolonging the functional duration of PVCs remains uncertain. Therefore, it is necessary to systematically review existing studies to provide evidence-based guidance for clinicians. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of different PVC dressings and securement devices on the incidence of PVC failure. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of electronic databases was conducted to identify relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The databases searched included the Cochrane Wounds Group Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, and EBSCO CINAHL, with the search completed in early 2015. Only RCTs or cluster RCTs comparing different dressings or securement devices for PVC stabilization were included. Cross-over trials were excluded unless data from the first treatment period were available. Two independent reviewers selected studies, assessed their quality, and extracted data. Missing information was sought by contacting the study authors. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were followed during the review process. The review included six RCTs involving a total of 1,539 participants. The sample sizes of the trials ranged from 50 to 703 participants. These trials compared four different interventions: transparent dressings versus gauze, bordered transparent dressings versus a securement device, bordered transparent dressings versus tape, and transparent dressings versus sticking plaster. The evidence from these studies was of very low quality. Two studies (278 participants) suggested that transparent dressings might result in fewer catheter dislodgements or accidental removals compared to gauze (relative risk [RR] 0.40; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.17 to 0.92; P = 0.03). However, the effects of transparent dressings versus gauze on phlebitis (RR 0.89; 95% CI 0.47 to 1.68) and infiltration (RR 0.80; 95% CI 0.48 to 1.33) were unclear. A single small study compared bordered transparent dressings with a securement device. This study provided very low-quality evidence suggesting that bordered transparent dressings might reduce the frequency of dislodgement or accidental catheter removal (RR 0.14; 95% CI 0.03 to 0.63). However, the same study indicated a higher incidence of phlebitis with bordered dressings (RR 8.11; 95% CI 1.03 to 64.02). Another small study compared bordered transparent dressings with tape. This study found very low-quality evidence suggesting that bordered transparent dressings might be associated with a higher rate of PVC failure (RR 1.84; 95% CI 1.08 to 3.11). However, the effects on catheter dislodgement were unclear. The comparison between transparent dressings and sticking plaster was evaluated in one small study, but the results were inconclusive. Overall, the evidence from these studies is insufficient to determine whether any specific dressing or securement device is superior for stabilizing PVCs. There is a clear need for additional high-quality, independent RCTs to evaluate both traditional and newer securement products. Given the significant cost differences between some of these products, future studies should also include robust cost-effectiveness analyses.
